newsitem.title: GERMANY: German CDU sell euro as joint front against dollar.
newsitem.headline: German CDU sell euro as joint front against dollar.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), facing a growing chorus of Euro-sceptics, on Tuesday unveiled a poster selling Europe's planned single currency, the euro, as a united front against the dollar.

The new advert came after weeks of bickering in the ruling coalition between Kohl's CDU and its conservative sister party in Bavaria, the Christian Social Union (CSU), over the euro and after surveys showed growing public opposition to it.
An opinion poll this month showed a slim majority of voters were now opposed to Germany adopting the euro fearing it might be weaker than the mark and could devalue their savings.

Since the beginning of the year the mark has lost 14 percent against the dollar which is now trading above 1.75 marks,and while Germany sticks to its plans to join economic and monetary union (EMU) analysts see no chance for this movement to be reversed.

CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said the poster entitled "The euro makes us strong" was intended to hit back at Germany's growing number of Euro-sceptics -- who have dubbed the euro an "esperanto currency".

"A strong European currency is essential to compete with other economic regions in a globalised economy," Hintze said, adding the poster was to be displayed strategically in 13,000 places all across the country.

"The European Union's monetary fragmentation into 14 currencies is a great economic disadvantage compared with the United States' single currency," Hintze said. "This poster aims to provoke citizens' to think about the euro's advantages".

The poster shows a map of the United States with number one printed on it alongside a map of Europe and the figure 14. The number one is filed in with the Stars and Stripes flag and the 14 with the EU symbol of stars on blue background.

A month-long simmering row between sister parties came to a head last week when Kohl came under intense pressure from his Bavarian colleagues to ensure Bonn would interpret entry criteria for EMU strictly to the decimal point.

Edmund Stoiber, the powerful premier of the large southern state and one of Germany's leading Euro-sceptics, insisted Bonn must interpret the three percent deficit-to-gross domestic product criteria as exactly 3.0 percent.

Kohl last week caved in to the pressure and said three meant 3.0, a pledge that would make it more difficult for Germany and certainly France to qualify in 1997 -- the crunch year in which fiscal data determine which countries qualify for EMU.

France has already said officially its budget deficit will be much higher than 3.0 percent and economic forecasts do not put Germany's deficit much lower, raising the prospect of a delay in the project -- something Kohl adamantly rejects.

Stoiber has also called for a "controlled delay" of the project rather than fudge the Maastricht criteria which he argues must be kept to strictly as a guarantee the new currency would be as strong and stable as the mark.

"This poster comes at a time when we hear sceptical noises from a government chief in southern Germany. We want to make it perfectly clear that Germany will help launch the euro on time and that a delay is out of the question," Hintze said.
